C0.1.q: You want a note to keep sounding while your hands adjust a control. What do you switch on?
C0.1.why: Hold keeps a note sounding after you let go, so your hands are free.

C0.1.q: You open the synth and click a key, but hear nothing. What is the most likely reason?
options: Audio has not been started yet
Keys only work from the computer keyboard
C0.1.why: Audio starts only after you click to start it.

C0.1.q: What does the starting patch sound like?
options: A tone that fades in slowly and fades out
Several notes sounding together on one key
A tone that rings on after every key
One plain steady tone that starts and stops instantly
C0.1.why: The starting patch is deliberately plain: one steady tone that starts and stops instantly.

C0.1.q: Hold is on and a note is sounding. You turn the volume down. What do you hear?
C0.1.why: Hold keeps the note sounding, so turning the volume down makes that same note quieter.

C0.1.q: You click a key with the mouse, then play a different note from the computer keyboard. What do you hear?
options: A brighter tone at the same pitch
The same tone at another pitch
C0.1.why: Both ways of playing give the same plain tone, just at the pitch of the key you choose.

options: How big the wave is on the scope
How many times the wave repeats each second
How long a note has been held
How many notes are sounding at once
C0.2.why: Frequency is the number of repeats per second, measured in hertz.

C0.2.q: As you drag the frequency up, the waves on the scope get narrower. What do you hear?
C0.2.why: More repeats per second sounds higher in pitch.

C0.2.q: A note is at 440 Hz. What frequency is the same note one octave down?
C0.2.why: Each octave is a doubling, so one octave down is half the frequency.

C0.2.q: You switch on Hold, play a note and leave everything alone. What does the wave on the scope do?
C0.2.why: A steady tone repeats the same way every time, so its wave stands still on the scope.

C0.2.q: You set the frequency to 220 Hz, then to 440 Hz. How does the second note compare with the first?
options: The same note, twice as loud
The same note, one octave higher
The same note, one octave lower
C0.2.why: Doubling the frequency gives the same note one octave up.

C0.3.q: You lower the volume by 6 dB, then by 6 dB again. How do the two steps compare?
options: The second step sounds far bigger
The second step cannot be heard
They sound like equal steps in loudness
Only the first step moves the meter
C0.3.why: Decibels are built on ratios, so equal decibel steps sound like equal steps in loudness.

C0.3.q: Roughly how big a drop in level sounds like half as loud?
C0.3.why: As a rule of thumb, roughly 10 dB sounds like twice or half as loud.

C0.3.q: Why set a comfortable listening level before working on sounds?
options: Quiet sounds have fewer harmonics in them
Loud listening tires your ears and hides detail
The meter only works at low levels
Loud notes drift higher in pitch
C0.3.why: Loud listening tires your ears and hides detail, so a comfortable level lets you hear more.

C0.3.q: You have lowered the volume by 6 dB twice. What brings back the loudness you started with?
C0.3.why: Two 6 dB steps down add up to 12 dB, so 12 dB up returns to the start.

C0.3.q: You are setting your device volume for a long session. Which level do you choose?
C0.3.why: A comfortable level is one you could talk over and hear for minutes at a time.

C0.4.q: Where do a pitched sound's harmonics sit?
options: All of them stacked exactly at the pitch you hear
One at the pitch you hear, others at whole multiples
All of them somewhere below the pitch you hear
Scattered up and down with no pattern at all
C0.4.why: A pitched sound is a stack of harmonics: one at the pitch you hear and others at whole multiples of it.

C0.4.q: Two sounds have the same pitch and the same loudness, yet sound different. Why?
options: They have a different mix of harmonics
One of them repeats faster each second
One of them has a bigger wave
One of them is held for longer
C0.4.why: Which harmonics are present, and how strong each is, gives a sound its colour.

C0.4.q: What makes a tone sound brighter?
options: A single peak on the spectrum
A bigger reading on the meter
C0.4.why: More and stronger high harmonics sound brighter.

C1.1.q: How does a triangle differ from a sine?
options: It adds every harmonic there is
It takes away the only harmonic
It adds a few quiet odd harmonics
C1.1.why: A sine is a single harmonic; a triangle adds a few quiet odd ones.

C1.1.q: A tone sounds hollow and every other peak is missing on the spectrum. Which shape is it?
C1.1.why: A square has strong odd harmonics, which sounds hollow.

C1.1.q: Why does a saw sound bright and full?
options: It is louder than the others
C1.1.why: A saw has every harmonic, which sounds bright and full.

C1.1.q: You play a low note on Sine through small speakers. What do you notice?
options: It is hollow like a clarinet
It is louder than a saw
C1.1.why: A sine has a single harmonic, so a low one is hard to hear on small speakers.

C1.1.q: You hold a note on Square, then switch to Saw. What changes on the spectrum?
options: The missing peaks appear, so every peak is present
Every other peak drops out, leaving gaps
All but one of the peaks drop out
The peaks stay put and only get taller
C1.1.why: A saw has every harmonic, so the peaks a square leaves out are all there.

C1.2.q: You want the same note, but down in the bass register. Which control do you reach for?
C1.2.why: Octave moves the oscillator in doublings, which sets its register.

C1.2.q: Semitone is set to +7. What do you hear when you press a key?
options: A different note, a fifth above the key
The same note, one octave higher
The same note, barely changed at all
The same note, in the bass register
C1.2.why: Semitone moves the oscillator in keyboard steps, so it makes intervals such as a fifth.

C1.2.q: When does Fine tuning make a difference you can really hear?
options: Whenever it is moved, as a new note
Only when Octave is set to 0
Only on notes in the bass register
When another sound is playing next to it
C1.2.why: Cents are too small to hear as a new note, so fine tune only matters next to another sound.

C1.2.q: You hold a middle note and set Octave to -1. What do you hear?
options: A different note, a fifth lower
C1.2.why: Octave moves the oscillator in doublings, so you get the same note in a lower register.

C1.2.q: You want the oscillator a few cents off, too little to hear as a new note. Which control do you use?
C1.2.why: Fine moves the oscillator in cents, which are too small to hear as a new note.

C1.M.q: When matching a hidden sound, in what order should you listen?
options: All three at the same moment
C1.M.why: Listen for one quality at a time: colour first, then register, then interval.

C1.M.q: What makes the differences between the target and your sound obvious?
options: Listening to the target for a long time
Playing each one on a different key
Turning both of them up louder
C1.M.why: Switching quickly between target and yours makes differences obvious.

C1.M.q: When you check your match, what does the app tell you?
options: The exact numbers of the target's settings
Only whether the whole sound matches or not
Which wave shape and octave the target uses
Which settings match, and which way the rest are off
C1.M.why: Being told too high or too low is enough to find the sound; the numbers stay hidden.

options: A second oscillator layered on top
A list of notes to play
C1.3.why: A wavetable is a row of single-cycle shapes, and the oscillator plays one at a time.

C1.3.q: What does the Position control do?
options: Moves the note up or down in octaves
Swaps the whole wavetable for a different one
Chooses which shape plays, blending between neighbours
Sets how loud the oscillator is playing
C1.3.why: Position picks one shape from the row and blends between neighbours.

C1.3.q: You hold a note and sweep Position from one end to the other. What happens to the pitch?
options: It rises as the colour gets brighter
It stays put while the colour changes
It jumps at each new shape
It falls as the colour gets duller
C1.3.why: Sweeping the position changes the harmonics smoothly while the pitch stays the same.

C1.3.q: You choose the Basic morph wavetable with Position at the very start. What do you hear?
C1.3.why: At the start of the Basic morph table the frame is a pure tone.

C1.3.q: You choose a different wavetable and sweep Position again. What do you hear?
options: A different kind of colour change
The very same colour change as before
A change in pitch, not in colour
No change, as Position stops working
C1.3.why: Each wavetable is its own row of shapes, so sweeping another one changes the colour in a different way.

C1.4.q: Osc B's semitone is set to +7. What does one key play now?
C1.4.why: At intervals other than the same pitch or an octave, one key plays two notes.

C1.4.q: Osc B, an octave up, should be only a quiet sheen above A. What do you adjust?
C1.4.why: The two levels are a small mix, so you balance B against A with its level.

C1.4.q: Two oscillators play at different levels. Which one sets the character of the sound?
C1.4.why: The louder oscillator defines the sound.

C1.4.q: You switch on Osc B at the same pitch and shape as A. What do you hear?
options: The same note in the bass
C1.4.why: A second oscillator at the same pitch thickens the tone, so it sounds louder and slightly fuller.

C1.4.q: You want Osc B to add brightness on top of A. How do you set it?
C1.4.why: Set one octave up, the second oscillator adds brightness above the first.

C1.5.q: Two oscillators are tuned a few cents apart. What do you hear?
C1.5.why: Two near-equal pitches drift in and out of step, adding then cancelling, which you hear as a repeating swell.

C1.5.q: What sets how fast the swell repeats?
options: The difference between the two frequencies
The level of the louder oscillator
The length of time the note is held
The wave shape of the two oscillators
C1.5.why: The swell repeats at a rate equal to the difference between the two frequencies.

C1.5.q: You keep the same gap in cents and play a key an octave higher. What does the beating do?
C1.5.why: The same gap in cents beats faster on higher notes.

C1.5.q: The swell is too slow for you. What do you do with the two Fine controls?
C1.5.why: A wider gap between the two pitches makes the beating faster.

C1.5.q: Both Fine controls are at 0 and you hold a low note. What do you hear?
C1.5.why: With no gap between the two pitches there is no beating, so the tone is steady.

C1.6.q: You raise Voices to 3 with Detune at zero. Why does the tone hardly change?
options: Unison needs seven voices to work
Spread has not been raised yet
C1.6.why: Unison stacks detuned copies, so with no detune the copies are identical and sound much the same.

C1.6.q: With Detune raised, what does going from 3 voices to 7 do to the sound?
options: Makes it sour and out of tune
C1.6.why: With many copies the individual beats average out into a smooth thickness.

C1.6.q: What happens when Detune is pushed too far?
options: The note sounds sour and its pitch blurs
The note goes silent as the copies cancel
The note moves over to one side
The note drops into the bass register
C1.6.why: Too much detune blurs the pitch, so back off to where it is thick but still in tune.

C1.6.q: You want the sound to open out to the sides. Which control do you raise?
C1.6.why: Spread places the copies across left and right, which adds width.

C1.6.q: With 3 voices on, you slowly raise Detune from zero. What appears in the sound?
C1.6.why: Detune spreads the copies slightly in pitch, and you hear that as a swirl.

C1.7.q: Why add a sub under detuned main oscillators?
options: It adds hiss and air on top
It stays steady and anchors the low end
It makes the detuned beating faster
It makes the main tone sound brighter
C1.7.why: The sub is a simple low tone that stays steady even when the main oscillators are detuned.

C1.7.q: Why does noise sound like breath or air and not like a note?
options: It plays one octave under the main pitch
It has only one harmonic, like a sine
It is always quieter than the sub
It has no pitch; its energy is spread out
C1.7.why: Noise has no pitch: its energy is spread across the spectrum.

C1.7.q: How loud should the sub and the noise usually be?
options: As loud as they will go
Exactly level with the main tone
C1.7.why: Both work best quiet, sitting under the main tone in proportion.

C1.7.q: You switch on the sub, one octave down. What appears on the spectrum?
options: A new peak at the far right
A fill across the whole spectrum
A gap where the main tone was
A new peak at the far left
C1.7.why: The sub is a low tone under the main pitch, so it shows as a new peak at the far left.

C1.7.q: White noise is on at a low level. You switch it to pink. What do you hear?
options: A low tone under the note
C1.7.why: Pink noise gives a darker, softer hiss than white noise.

options: How many cycles a wave makes each second
How big a wave is on the scope
Where in its cycle a wave starts
How far left or right a wave sits
C1.8.why: Phase is where in its cycle a wave starts.

C1.8.q: You want every bass note to hit in exactly the same way. What do you set?
C1.8.why: With fixed phase every note begins identically, which is tight and repeatable.

C1.8.q: Two identical square waves play half a cycle apart. What do you hear?
C1.8.why: Opposite phases cancel when the two waves are otherwise identical.

C1.8.q: Random phase is at 100% and you strike one note four times. What do you hear?
C1.8.why: With random phase each note begins somewhere different in its cycle, so the starts vary.

C1.8.q: Moving Osc B's phase to 180° made the sound almost vanish. How do you get full level back?
options: Strike the note four more times
Bring B's phase back to match A
C1.8.why: When the two phases are equal the waves add, so the full level returns.

C1.9.q: Osc A's Pan is at -100. Where do you hear it?
C1.9.why: Pan at 0 is the middle; -100 is only the left speaker and 100 only the right.

C1.9.q: Osc A is panned to about -40 and Osc B to about +40. How does it sound?
options: Like one sound in the middle only
Like one sound on the right only
Like one wide sound with a middle
C1.9.why: Partly apart sounds like one wide thing; fully apart often sounds like two.

C1.9.q: A is panned left, B right. You sweep Osc B's wavetable Position. What changes?
options: The tone on both sides together
C1.9.why: Osc B has its own wavetable and position, independent of Osc A's.

C1.C.q: What is the best way to listen to a hidden target sound?
options: Take one quality at a time
Listen only for how loud it is
C1.C.why: Take one quality at a time: pitch content, thickness, weight, then brightness.

C1.C.q: You cannot tell how your sound differs from the target. What helps most?
options: Listening to the target for longer
Playing each on a different key
C1.C.why: Quick switching between target and yours beats long listening.

C1.C.q: The check says one of your settings is too high. What do you do?
options: Wait for the app to show the number
Reset every setting and start over
Lower it a little and check again
Raise it further and check again
C1.C.why: Being told too high or too low is enough to home in, without the numbers.
